drivingQuestion: What is Beit Shammai's reason for not reading the verse as Beit Hillel do, and what does each school derive from ובלכתך בדרך?
outcomeNote: Both schools are given a rationale and a use for ובלכתך בדרך: Beit Shammai excluding agents of a mitzva, Beit Hillel deriving from the same exclusion that all others recite even on the road.

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ בִּשְׁלָמָא בֵּית הִלֵּל — קָא מְפָרְשִׁי טַעְמַיְיהוּ וְטַעְמָא דְּבֵית שַׁמַּאי, אֶלָּא בֵּית שַׁמַּאי — מַאי טַעְמָא לָא אָמְרִי כְּבֵית הִלֵּל?
segments.en: «GEMARA:» The Gemara begins by clarifying the rationale for Beit Shammai’s opinion. «Granted, Beit Hillel explain the rationale» for «their» opinion «and the rationale for Beit Shammai’s» opinion«.» Beit Hillel explain both the verse that ostensibly supports Beit Shammai’s opinion: When you lie down«,» at the time when people lie down«,» etc«.,» and the verse that proves that their own explanation is more reasonable: “And when you walk along the way.” «However, what is the reason that Beit Shammai do not state» their opinion «in accordance with» the opinion of «Beit Hillel?»

segments.he: אָמְרִי לָךְ בֵּית שַׁמַּאי: אִם כֵּן, נֵימָא קְרָא ״בַּבֹּקֶר וּבָעֶרֶב״, מַאי ״בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ״? בִּשְׁעַת שְׁכִיבָה — שְׁכִיבָה מַמָּשׁ, וּבִשְׁעַת קִימָה — קִימָה מַמָּשׁ.
segments.en: The Gemara answers, «Beit Shammai» could «have said to you: If so» that the verse means only to denote the time for the recitation of Shema, as claimed by Beit Hillel, «then let the verse say: “In the morning and in the evening.” What» is the meaning of the ambiguous formulation: «“When you lie down, and when you rise”?» It must mean that «at the time of lying down» one must recite Shema while «actually lying down, and at the time of arising» one must recite Shema while «actually risen.»

segments.he: וּבֵית שַׁמַּאי: הַאי ״וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ״, מַאי עֲבִיד לְהוּ?
segments.en: The Gemara continues, asking: «And what do Beit Shammai do with this» verse: «“And when you walk along the way,”» which Beit Hillel use to prove that every person recites Shema as he is?

segments.he: הָהוּא מִבְּעֵי לְהוּ, לְכִדְתַנְיָא: ״בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ בְּבֵיתֶךָ״ — פְּרָט לְעוֹסֵק בְּמִצְוָה, ״וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ״ — פְּרָט לְחָתָן. מִכָּאן, אָמְרוּ: הַכּוֹנֵס אֶת הַבְּתוּלָה — פָּטוּר, וְאֶת הָאַלְמָנָה — חַיָּיב.
segments.en: The Gemara answers: Beit Shammai «need this» verse in order to derive other halakhot, «as it was taught» in a baraita which interpreted this verse that the obligation to recite Shema applies «when you sit in your home, to the exclusion of one who is engaged in» performance of «a mitzva,» who is exempt from the recitation of Shema; «and when you walk along the way, to the exclusion of a groom,» who is also exempt from the recitation of Shema. The baraita adds that «from here,» from this interpretation of the verses, «they said: One who marries a virgin is exempt» from the recitation of Shema on his wedding night, «but one who marries a widow is obligated.»
The Gemara clarifies the meaning of this baraita, and asks: «From where may it be inferred» that the verse, when you walk along the way, exempts a groom from the obligation to recite Shema?

segments.he: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּי דֶרֶךְ. מָה דֶּרֶךְ רְשׁוּת, אַף כֹּל רְשׁוּת.
segments.en: «Rav Pappa said» that we learn: «Like the way; just as» the journey along a specific «way» described in the verse «is voluntary» and involves no mitzva, «so too all» of those who are obligated to recite Shema are engaged in «voluntary» activities. However, one engaged in the performance of a mitzva, like a groom, is exempt from the obligation to recite Shema.

segments.he: מִי לָא עָסְקִינַן דְּקָא אָזֵיל לִדְבַר מִצְוָה, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא: לִקְרֵי. אִם כֵּן לִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא ״בְּשֶׁבֶת וּבְלֶכֶת״ מַאי ״בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ״? — בְּשֶׁבֶת דִּידָךְ וּבְלֶכֶת דִּידָךְ הוּא דְּמִחַיְּיבַתְּ, הָא דְּמִצְוָה פְּטִירַתְּ.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «Are we not dealing with» a case where «one walks» along the way «to perform a mitzva?» The Torah did not designate the objective of his walk and, «nevertheless, the Torah said to recite» Shema, indicating that one is obligated even if he set out to perform a mitzva. Rather, the proof is from the formulation of the verse. «If so,» that the intention was to obligate in all cases, «let the Torah write: When sitting and when walking. What is» the meaning of: «When you sit and when you walk?» Certainly these additions come to emphasize «in your sitting down and in your walking,» meaning that when one does this for his own purposes and of his own volition, «he is obligated» to recite Shema, «but» when he does with the objective of performing «a mitzva, he is exempt» from reciting Shema, as in that case he is sitting or walking at God’s behest.

segments.he: אִי הָכִי אֲפִילּוּ כּוֹנֵס אֶת הָאַלְמָנָה נָמֵי?
segments.en: The conclusion is that anyone engaged in the performance of a mitzva is exempt from the recitation of Shema. «If so, even one who marries a widow should be» exempt, for he, too, is engaged in performance of a mitzva. That, however, contradicts the baraita.

The Gemara responds that there is nevertheless a distinction between one marrying a virgin and one marrying a widow. «One» who marries a virgin «is preoccupied» by his concern lest he discover that his bride is not a virgin, while «one» who marries a widow «is not preoccupied.» The conclusion is that the groom is exempt from reciting Shema because he is preoccupied.

segments.he: אִי מִשּׁוּם טִרְדָּא, אֲפִילּוּ טָבְעָה סְפִינָתוֹ בַּיָּם נָמֵי! וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָכִי נָמֵי, אַלְּמָה אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא אָמַר רַב: אָבֵל חַיָּיב בְּכָל הַמִּצְוֹת הָאֲמוּרוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה, חוּץ מִן הַתְּפִילִּין, שֶׁהֲרֵי נֶאֱמַר בָּהֶם ״פְּאֵר״, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״פְּאֵרְךָ חֲבוֹשׁ עָלֶיךָ״?!
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «If» the exemption is «due to preoccupation,» then «even one» who is preoccupied because «his ship sank at sea» should «also» be exempt. The Gemara reinforces its question: «And if you say» that «in this case as well,» when one’s ship sank at sea, one is exempt, «why» then «did Rabbi Abba bar Zavda say» that «Rav said: A mourner is obligated in all the mitzvot mentioned in the Torah except for» the mitzva to don «phylacteries,» from which a mourner is exempt, «as» the term «splendor is stated» with regard to phylacteries, «as it is stated:» “Make no mourning for the dead, «bind your splendor upon yourself”» (Ezekiel 24:17). It is inappropriate for a mourner to wrap himself in phylacteries, with regard to which, the term splendor was employed (Tosafot). If a mourner, who is clearly pained and preoccupied, is obligated to recite Shema, then certainly all others who are preoccupied, even one whose ship sank at sea, whose loss was merely monetary (Birkat Hashem), should be obligated. Why, then, is a groom exempted because of his preoccupation and one who lost his property is not?

segments.he: הָתָם טְרִיד טִרְדָּא דְמִצְוָה, הָכָא טְרִיד טִרְדָּא דִרְשׁוּת.
segments.en: The Gemara answers: Nevertheless, there is a distinction between the cases. For «there,» in the case of a groom, «he is preoccupied with the preoccupation of a mitzva» that he must perform; «here,» in the case of a ship lost at sea, «he is preoccupied with the preoccupation of a voluntary» act that he chooses to perform.
Here, the Gemara returns to its initial question: «And» how do «Beit Shammai» explain the passage: “When you walk along the way” (Rashash)?

segments.he: הָהוּא מִבְּעֵי לְהוּ — פְּרָט לִשְׁלוּחֵי מִצְוָה.
segments.en: The Gemara answers: Beit Shammai «need this» passage in order to «exclude one who is on the path» to perform «a mitzva» from the obligation to recite Shema.

segments.he: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אָמְרִי: מִמֵּילָא שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ דַּאֲפִילּוּ בַדֶּרֶךְ נָמֵי קָרֵי.
segments.en: Beit Hillel also agree that one engaged in the performance of a mitzva is exempt from reciting Shema? If so, the halakha that they derived from: When you walk along the way lacks a source and is therefore unfounded. «And Beit Hillel say: Derive from this» halakha «itself» that one who is not an agent in the performance of a mitzva «recites» Shema «even along the way.»

moves.summary: the Gemara grants that Beit Hillel account for both verses and asks what Beit Shammai's reason is
moves.about: Beit Hillel account for both their own verse and Beit Shammai's, whereas Beit Shammai's position is left without a rationale

moves.summary: the setama answers for Beit Shammai: a mere time marker would have read 'in the morning and in the evening'
moves.about: the defence the setama supplies for Beit Shammai: had the verse meant only to fix the time it would have said 'in the morning and in the evening'

moves.summary: it asks what Beit Shammai do with the clause 'and when you walk along the way'
moves.about: what Beit Shammai do with the clause ובלכתך בדרך, on which Beit Hillel rely

moves.summary: they need it for the baraita that excludes one engaged in a mitzva and a bridegroom
moves.about: Beit Shammai need the clause for the baraita's derivation exempting one engaged in a mitzva and a bridegroom

moves.cueHe: מכאן אמרו: הכונס את הבתולה פטור
moves.summary: the baraita's practical upshot: one who marries a virgin is exempt from Shema, one who marries a widow obligated
moves.about: בשבתך בביתך excludes one engaged in a mitzva and ובלכתך בדרך excludes a bridegroom, whence one who marries a virgin is exempt and one who marries a widow is obligated

moves.summary: it asks how the exemption of a bridegroom is inferred from the verse
moves.about: from where in the wording it may be inferred that ובלכתך בדרך exempts a bridegroom

moves.summary: Rav Pappa answers that the way is voluntary, so the obligation speaks only of voluntary activity
moves.about: the derivation works because the way is voluntary, so the whole obligation speaks of voluntary activity

moves.summary: it objects that one may walk the way for a mitzva and is still commanded to recite
moves.about: whether דרך can prove the exemption, since one may also be walking the way in order to perform a mitzva and the Torah still commanded him to recite

moves.cueHe: אם כן לכתוב רחמנא בשבת ובלכת
moves.summary: the derivation is relocated to the possessive forms: your sitting and your walking obligate, a mitzva's does not
moves.about: the possessive forms בשבתך ובלכתך show that only sitting and walking of one's own volition obligate, while going for a mitzva exempts

moves.summary: then one who marries a widow should be exempt too, contrary to the baraita
moves.about: if anyone engaged in a mitzva is exempt, one who marries a widow should be exempt too, against the baraita

moves.summary: the one is preoccupied and the other is not
moves.about: the exemption turns on preoccupation: one marrying a virgin is preoccupied and one marrying a widow is not

moves.summary: if preoccupation exempts, one whose ship sank at sea should be exempt as well
moves.about: if mere preoccupation exempts, then one whose ship sank at sea should be exempt as well

moves.summary: the concession that he too is exempt is floated and knocked down from Rav's ruling that a mourner is obligated in all mitzvot
moves.about: the floated concession that one whose ship sank is indeed exempt, knocked down from Rav's ruling that a mourner is obligated in all the mitzvot

moves.summary: preoccupation with a mitzva exempts, preoccupation with a voluntary matter does not
moves.about: the bridegroom is preoccupied with the preoccupation of a mitzva, the man whose ship sank with the preoccupation of a voluntary matter

moves.summary: the Gemara returns to what Beit Shammai themselves derive from the clause
moves.about: the standing question, now returned to: what Beit Shammai derive from ובלכתך בדרך, since the baraita's derivation belongs to Beit Hillel

moves.cueHe: ההוא מבעי להו — פרט לשלוחי מצוה
moves.summary: they need it to exclude agents sent to perform a mitzva
moves.about: Beit Shammai need ובלכתך בדרך to exclude those on the way to perform a mitzva

moves.cueHe: ובית הלל אמרי: ממילא שמע מינה
moves.summary: Beit Hillel answer that once the agents of a mitzva are excluded, it follows of itself that everyone else recites even on the road
moves.about: once agents of a mitzva are excluded it follows of itself that everyone else recites even while on the way
